sentences.text: Revenue compounded at 5.4% a year from $114 billion in FY2016 to $184 billion in FY2025 [F1][F10][F177], but the path was cyclical rather than a trend.
The window's two step changes were FY2021, when revenue rose 64.7% [F6][D192], and FY2022, when it rose a further 51.5% to $236 billion [F7][D232].
Those increases were driven by higher upstream realizations and downstream margins [P55][P56][P57].

Revenue then fell in each of FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025, down 16.5%, 1.8% and 4.6% [F8][F9][F10][D274][D316][D358], with the latest decline attributed to lower crude oil and refined product prices [P17].
The company's top line is a price signal more than a growth engine; the ten-year CAGR mostly reflects where the commodity cycle started and ended [F177].
Chevron U.S.A. Inc. supplied 75.1% of FY2025 revenue [S9][D402] and subtracted 3.9pp from growth as it fell 5.3% [D403][D404].
Tengizchevroil was the offset, growing 16.5% and adding 1.5pp, lifting its share to 11.6% [S15][D418][D419][D420].
Higher TCO liftings from the FGP project and the Hess acquisition lifted production 12% [P28][P22], though TCO's equity earnings fell on higher DD&A and lower realizations [P16].
Operating costs fell 3.4% against a 4.6% revenue decline, so the incremental margin was negative [X60][D373][D358][D379].
Diluted EPS fell 31.8% against a 30.5% fall in net income [F50][D361][F20][D359], as the diluted share count rose 2.1% on the Hess share issuance [X122][D374].
Net margin of 6.7% in FY2025 [F30] sits below the 7.9% window median and far below the 15.1% FY2022 high [D613][D612], though above the -5.9% FY2020 low [D611].
The 2.5pp net-margin decline in FY2025 [D369] came from higher upstream DD&A and lower realizations [P9], with DD&A up to $20.1 billion from $17.3 billion [X70][X69][P12].
SG&A rose 6.0% to $5.1 billion [X50][D372], which the filing attributes to the Hess acquisition and higher professional service costs [P13].
The effective tax rate rose to 36.8% from 35.5% [D345][D303], widening the gap between operating and net margin; the filing warns the rate moves with earnings mix [P33].
Cost of revenue at 57.2% of revenue [D338] is the swing factor: it peaked at 59.3% in FY2023 [D254] and any price recovery flows through it quickly.
Operating cash flow of $33.9 billion was 2.76x net income [F60][F20][D346], well above the 1.97x window median [D644], as DD&A absorbed much of the earnings decline.
Free cash flow was $16.6 billion, an 8.8% margin [F80][D343], against a 8.9% window median [D616].
Operating cash rose 7.8% [D362] as higher TCO distributions and legacy Hess assets offset lower commodity prices [P6].
Capex of $17.3 billion was 9.2% of revenue and 0.86x D&A [F70][D342][D348], with FY2026 organic capex guided at $18-19 billion [P4].
Cash and investments were $7.3 billion at FY2025 [D349], and total assets jumped 26.1% to $324 billion [F110][D365], largely the Hess acquisition.
Debt issued was $11.4 billion in FY2025 [X157], and interest expense rose to $1.2 billion from $594 million [X80][X79].
Return on average equity of 7.3% [D357] ranks in the 17th percentile of six energy peers against a 14.9% median [D641][D642].
Buybacks and dividends of $24.8 billion were 149.7% of free cash flow [D353][D354], with $12.1 billion of buybacks [X132] and $12.8 billion of dividends [X142].
Revenue has fallen for three straight years, from $197 billion in FY2023 to $184 billion in FY2025 [F8][F10][R1], a persistent top-line contraction.
Payouts have exceeded free cash flow for three years, at 132.8%, 179.7% and 149.7% [D270][D312][D354][R4], funded partly by balance-sheet capacity.

The revenue series mixes presentations: FY2025 is $184 billion in the table versus $189 billion as first reported [F10][X10][R3], so growth and margin comparisons across the break are not like-for-like.
Long-term debt is not reported after FY2021 [X193][R12], so net-cash and debt-growth figures after that year are incomplete and I have not relied on them.
Net margin: a move back above the 7.9% window median [D613] would confirm the cost and price trend has turned; a print below the 6.7% FY2025 level [F30] would extend the decline.
Free cash flow against the $16.6 billion FY2025 level [F80]: coverage of the $24.8 billion payout [D353] requires FCF above that figure, otherwise buybacks must shrink.
Capex against the $18-19 billion FY2026 guidance [P4] versus $17.3 billion in FY2025 [F70]: spending above the top of the range without matching cash flow would pressure the payout.
